Driven by a shared passion for cutting-edge technology, our team focuses on designing next-generation orbital systems, advanced satellite concepts, and trajectory solutions.
summary:
ASTRA (Astronaut Safety, Tracking & Risk Assessment) is a local-first health-monitoring prototype for long-duration missions, where delayed Earth support leaves astronauts interpreting their own health changes. Instead of generic thresholds, ASTRA compares each astronaut with their own baseline and raises a WATCH or REVIEW alert only after sustained changes in resting heart rate, skin temperature or sleep. Low-quality readings, such as motion artifacts, never trigger alerts. Every alert is explainable, showing its evidence, comparison window and model version. ASTRA never diagnoses.

The dashboard combines wearable readings with daily self-reported check-ins (sleep, mood, stress, fatigue) and states plainly which domains are not measured, such as radiation and bone health. An explainable Random Forest model trained on public wearable datasets (WESAD, PhysioNet) supports the analysis.

The backend is a validated, source-labelled FastAPI service with automated tests. Demo data is synthetic and labelled. NASA Human Research Program material informed the hazards we address. The CrewBand wristband is a design concept only.
details:
On a long mission, help from Earth can be delayed by many minutes. That means astronauts have to make sense of their own health changes. ASTRA is a prototype that helps with this. Instead of comparing an astronaut to a generic “normal” range, it learns that person’s own baseline from their first 14 days. It then warns them only when resting heart rate, skin temperature or sleep stays off that baseline for a while.

A single odd reading doesn’t trigger anything. A WATCH alert needs two valid readings in a row, and a REVIEW alert needs three. Readings with poor signal quality, such as motion noise, can never raise an alert. Every alert shows the evidence behind it, the time window it was compared against, and the model version. The astronaut can acknowledge the alert and log what they did about it. We also added a short daily check-in for sleep, mood, stress and fatigue.

ASTRA never diagnoses anything. The thresholds are demo assumptions that we chose ourselves.

Why it matters

Crews need early signals they can understand and judge for themselves, not a black box. We also made the dashboard say clearly what it does not measure: bone and muscle health, immune function, radiation and cabin environment. We didn’t want anyone to read silence as safety.

What is different about it

  • Each person is compared to themselves, not to a population average.
  • Persistence rules and the quality gate keep false alarms down.
  • A simple data-source adapter lets a future wristband plug in without changing the rest of the system.
  • The dashboard is honest about what is “not connected” instead of looking complete.

How we built it

Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, NumPy and pytest for the backend and analytics, with SQLite for storage (PostgreSQL). The frontend uses TypeScript, React and Vite, and is hosted on Vercel.

Data

All demo data is synthetic. We generated eight kinds of scenarios with fixed random seeds: stable, gradual drift, noise, dropout, missing data, repeated deviation and a few more. NASA Human Research Program material gave us the scientific background for the hazards.

Evidence

Our automated test suite has [N] passing tests. We also compared ASTRA with a simple “mean plus or minus 2 SD” rule over 200 random seeds of synthetic data. ASTRA gave [X]% false alarms against [Y]% for the simple rule. It detected [Z]% of real changes, with a median delay of [D] days. These numbers come from synthetic data only, so they don’t show how it would perform on real astronauts.

Use of Super Intelligence

We used Claude and Claude Code (Anthropic) to help debug the code, create tests and draft documents and slide text. ChatGPT helped us brainstorm ideas, and Perplexity helped with background research. The team ran, tested and reviewed all the code.
